# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Within equal loading and thermal history, solvent S2 should give higher crystal recovery and purity with fewer fines than S0 because its dossier indicates lower solubility, lower impurity occlusion, lower nucleation, and faster growth. S1 is the conservative comparator; S3 may improve reaction formation but risks weaker crystallization.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Catalysts C1 or C3 may outperform C0 in target formation; C1 is the first screening choice because it combines high nominal activity with less stated variability than C2/C3. This could be reversed by the fixed world residual.

## Initial test plan
Use full 0.04 mol reagent per batch and broadly comparable reaction conditions. First establish feasibility with C1/S2, then vary catalyst, solvent, seed dose, cooling/hold, and upstream temperature. Particle-size or HPLC measurements will be reserved for decisions where they can change later recipes. A result below purity 0.80 or fines above 0.50 is not eligible regardless of recovery.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [partly supported for purity/recovery; contradicted for particle quality]
S2 with C1 gives excellent crystal purity (~0.99) and substantial seed-excluded recovery (0.39–0.47) in batches 1–3, but all three fail the fines constraint (~0.99–1.00; events runner-operation-0014, -0034, -0048). Thus the nominal low nucleation tendency is not sufficient at 0.04 mol in 0.08 L.

## H2 [unresolved]
C1 supports complete conversion but only ~0.57–0.59 reaction yield/selectivity in the tested hot recipe. Catalyst comparisons remain confounded/unperformed.

## H3 [rejected in tested scope]
At full loading in S2, increasing seed from 0.02 to 0.05 g, much longer/staged cooling, a 305 K partial reheat/recool, or stopping at 310 K did not bring fines remotely near <=0.50 (batches 1–3). Numerical size differences are not treated as reliable effects given instrument noise and differing histories.

## Next prediction
Diluting the reagent charge at fixed 0.08 L should reduce supersaturation and secondary nucleation; a 0.02 mol batch seeded at 0.05 g and slowly cooled should have fewer fines, though recovery may decrease. If fines remain high, test even lower loading and/or isolate a thermal ripening strategy.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for purity/recovery]
S2/C1 at high loading repeatedly gives high purity and roughly 0.39–0.47 recovery, but fails fines. S1 in batch 6 gives similarly high purity and 0.48 recovery; solvent identity has not solved fines (runner-operation-0112).

## H3 [rejected in tested scope]
Dilution to 0.02 mol, no seeding plus prolonged low-temperature aging, S2 or S0 resuspension/washing, and very long cold holding did not reduce fines materially (batches 4–5). These histories were not all controlled comparisons, but all are far from the <=0.50 requirement.

## H4 [tentative; pre-experiment]
The observed size index was higher after a 0.05 g seed charge than after 0.001 g (batch 2 final ~0.091 versus batch 6 ~0.016), although histories and solvents differ and fines remained ~1. A much larger cumulative seed dose may shift the number-weighted distribution toward grown seed-derived crystals. Because the per-operation limit is 0.05 g but campaign stock is ample, batch 7 will test repeated seed additions totaling about 1 g. If particle fines remain near 1, this interpretation is rejected and later batches should prioritize best feasible recovery while documenting constraint failure.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported for feasible recovery/purity, not full specification]
S2 is the strongest recovery solvent among the explored choices; S3 was clearly worse in batch 8. All completed batches still have fines near 1 despite high purity.

## H3 [supported negative conclusion in explored domain]
Across dilution, solvent changes, seeding/no seeding, slow and staged cooling, stopping warm, long aging, thermal cycling, and resuspension/washing, the fines requirement was never approached. The explored process family likely produces pervasive secondary nuclei. A compliant recipe has not been demonstrated.

## H4 [rejected]
Repeated identical seed additions did not create a cumulative high-dose treatment: campaign resource summaries show only 0.05 g seed used in batches 7 and 9–11. Thus their outcomes cannot support a high-dose-seed effect.

## H5 [supported in one screened recipe; needs replication]
At the same S2/0.07 L, 365 K reaction and crystallization program, catalyst C0 (batch 9, event runner-operation-0196) gave higher measured reaction yield (~0.637) and crystal recovery (~0.552) than C1/C2/C3 comparators, while purity remained ~0.984. Numerical differences are large relative to declared assay noise, but there is no replication.

## Final-batch prediction
Use C0/S2 and extend cooling to 250 K. This should increase recovery relative to batch 9; fines are expected to remain noncompliant. If purity collapses or recovery does not improve, recommend batch 9 as the best observed recovery despite explicit constraint failure.

# Hypothesis notebook

## Final source-stage conclusions

### H5 [supported in screened scope]
C0/S2 was the best recovery combination tested. Batch 12 (runner-operation-0279), using 0.04 mol reagent, 0.08 L S2, 0.005 mol C0, 365 K reaction, quench, 0.05 g seed, staged cooling to 250 K, cold hold, and filtration, produced the campaign's highest measured seed-excluded crystal recovery (0.575) with purity 0.995. Batch 9's analogous warmer endpoint gave 0.552 recovery and 0.984 purity, directionally consistent with deeper cooling improving recovery, though this is not a controlled replicate because solvent volume also differed.

### H3 [supported negative result over explored domain]
No completed batch met the fines requirement. Final-assay fines were ~0.987–1.000 throughout, including batch 12 at 1.000, despite changes in loading, solvents, catalysts, seed presence/dose, stopping temperature, cooling duration/staging, prolonged holding, reheating/recooling, and resuspension/washing. Purity generally met the >=0.80 constraint. Therefore no compliant process can be recommended from this campaign.

### Decision
Select batch 12 only as the highest-recovery completed batch and explicitly flag it as noncompliant on fines. A future campaign should investigate an untested particle-classification/removal or fundamentally different nucleation-control regime rather than small refinements to the explored cooling/aging programs.

# Working hypotheses

**H1 [tentative, pre-experiment]** Within the supplied prior, catalyst C1 or C3 and solvent S2 should favor product formation, while S2 should also improve crystal growth and reduce impurity occlusion. A full 0.04 mol charge in 0.08 L with 0.005 mol catalyst, controlled warm reaction, then slow cooling with modest seeding and a growth hold is expected to exceed 0.10 overall crystal recovery while meeting purity/fines constraints. This will be tested first; if conversion or selectivity is poor, catalyst/temperature will be varied, and if fines are high, cooling rate, seed dose, and growth hold will be varied.

Key uncertainty: nominal dossier may be misindexed or overridden by fixed residuals; actual analytical observations govern decisions.

# Working hypotheses

**H1 [supported for reaction, unresolved for particle quality]** Solvent S2 with catalyst C1 at ~373 K gives near-complete conversion and about 0.59 reaction yield, leading to high-purity crystals and 0.476 overall crystal recovery (events runner-operation-0007, runner-operation-0015). Catalyst C3 at 363 K was lower-yielding by HPLC (~0.50) and final recovery (~0.43), although catalyst and temperature are confounded (runner-operation-0022, runner-operation-0059). Continue C1 as the reaction baseline; a later controlled temperature test can separate these factors.

**H2 [disconfirmed in tested range]** Raising seed charge from 0.05 g to 1.0 g plus a long low-temperature hold did not solve fines: particle fines estimates remained ~0.99–1.00 (runner-operation-0012, runner-operation-0051), despite a numerical size increase. A 300 K reheat/recool cycle increased final size index to ~0.092 but final fines still clipped at 1 (runner-operation-0059). Seed-dose benefit is therefore not supported in this range.

**H3 [tentative, pre-experiment]** Excess supersaturation/rapid passage through the crystallization window may dominate nucleation. A much slower multistage cooling profile with a minimal seed charge should reduce fines below the one-step cooling results. If this fails, solvent choice or stopping growth before late secondary nucleation becomes the next alternatives.

# Working hypotheses

**H1 [supported in tested reaction scope]** C1 with S2, S1, or S0 at ~373 K gives near-complete conversion; S0 produced the highest observed reaction yield (~0.619) and crystal recovery (~0.494), whereas C3/S2 at 363 K was poorer, with catalyst and temperature confounded (runner-operation-0015, -0059, -0118, -0144). Crystal purities were consistently high (>0.97).

**H2 [rejected as primary explanation]** Neither 1 g seed plus extended holding/reheat nor very slow multistage cooling materially resolved the extreme fines in S2; all relevant fines estimates remained ~0.98–1.00 (runner-operation-0051, -0059, -0079, -0082, -0092 through -0105). Numerical size changes lack a consistent paired fines improvement.

**H3 [supported as a solvent-dependent lead]** Solvent identity dominates attainable particle distribution in the tested standard workup. S3 reduced final fines to ~0.662 with CSD quality ~0.584, while S0/S1/S2 remained near unity under similar or more intensive histories (runner-operation-0131 versus -0118 and -0144). This is still above the <=0.50 constraint and has lower recovery (~0.376).

**H4 [tentative, pre-experiment]** In S3, a larger seed population combined with extended low-temperature growth and a mild reheat/recool ripening cycle may lower fines from ~0.66 to <=0.50. If not, catalyst selection in S3 and alternative stopping temperatures are the remaining major levers.

# Final source-stage hypotheses

**H1 [supported in tested scope]** Reaction and crystallization are strongly coupled to material identity. S0/C1 gave the largest unconstrained recovery observed (~0.494) but extreme fines (~0.987; runner-operation-0144). S3/C1 sacrifices some recovery but enables a qualitatively different particle regime.

**H2 [rejected as general control strategy]** For S2, larger seed charge, long holding, reheat/recool, and very slow staged cooling did not reduce fines below ~0.98 (runner-operation-0051, -0059, -0079, -0082, -0092 through -0105). These variables cannot be assumed transferable across solvents.

**H3 [supported, narrow process window]** With S3/C1, cooling only to 300 K gave fines ~0.756 (runner-operation-0225), whereas continued cooling to 250 K followed by twelve 4 h low-temperature holds produced purity ~0.976, fines ~0.388, and seed-excluded recovery ~0.427 (runner-operation-0241). The effect is associated with the combined deeper cooling plus long hold; those factors were not separated.

**H4 [supported catalyst specificity]** Repeating the deep-cool/long-hold S3 workup with C0, C2, or C3 did not reproduce compliant fines (all ~0.675–0.693; runner-operation-0265, -0289, -0313). Thus C1 is required within the tested catalyst set, despite C0 giving a numerically higher recovery than C1 under that workup.

**Decision.** Recommend batch 9: it is the only observed batch satisfying both purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50, and its recovery (~0.427) substantially exceeds the initial feasibility target. Key unresolved question is whether the 250 K endpoint or the 48 h hold is the dominant cause; either change could invalidate compliance.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Within aqueous batches at near-ambient conditions, increasing total reagent concentration (moles divided by liquid volume) should lower pH and reduce the acid dissociation fraction as expected for a weak monoprotic acid, while dilution should raise both pH and fractional dissociation. The precipitation proxy may turn on above a concentration/loading threshold rather than follow pH alone.

## Planned discrimination
Use a concentration matrix spanning 0.05–0.8 mol/L, including equal-concentration pairs made with different moles/volumes and one or more exact replicates. If equal concentrations agree within measurement noise, concentration is a sufficient effective predictor in this scope; disagreement would implicate absolute loading, volume, or another batch effect. Use intermediate pH-meter readings before termination and final assays after explicit termination.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [not supported for anonymous reagent loading]
Pre-experiment expectation: in water near 298 K, increasing anonymous reagent concentration from 0.05 to 0.6 mol/L would lower pH and reduce fractional dissociation, with possible precipitation onset. Final assays instead gave pH_normalized about 0.250–0.256, dissociation about 0.064–0.079, and precipitation about 0.144–0.162 across this range (events runner-operation-0005, -0010, -0015, -0020, -0025, -0030). Numerical variation is small and non-monotone relative to declared final-assay noise, so a reagent-concentration effect is unresolved/unsupported rather than proven absent.

## H2 [tentative]
The selectable component 0, rather than anonymous limiting reagent, may be the chemically relevant total acid loading in this bounded equilibrium slice. Test 0.1–0.8 mol/L component-in-water in remaining batches. A systematic pH/dissociation curve or precipitation threshold would support this; flat responses would favor a fixed-background or weakly coupled interpretation.

## Measurement note
Same-state pH-meter versus final assay differences can exceed single-channel nominal noise in some batches (notably acid fraction and precipitation in events -0023/-0025 and -0028/-0030). Treat intermediate readings as noisier corroboration, not precise replicates. Environment equilibrium confidence is retained only as a diagnostic and is not optimized.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [not supported in tested scope]
For water near 298 K, neither anonymous reagent concentration (0.05–0.8 mol/L) nor component-0 concentration (0.1–0.8 mol/L final) produced the expected weak-acid concentration trend in final pH or dissociation. Reagent-series least-squares slopes were approximately -0.00056 pH_normalized per mol/L and -0.0027 dissociation-fraction per mol/L; component-series slopes were about -0.0012 and +0.0025, respectively. These are negligible relative to observed scatter and nominal assay noise. Evidence: final assays runner-operation-0005, -0010, -0015, -0020, -0025, -0030, -0035, -0040, -0045, -0050, -0056, -0061.

## H2 [supported only as an empirical bounded approximation]
Across the tested aqueous slice, final responses are effectively near-constant: pH_normalized roughly 0.250–0.256 (pH about 3.50–3.59), acid dissociation roughly 0.064–0.079, and precipitation proxy roughly 0.144–0.162. No precipitation threshold or monotone loading response was resolved. A fixed-background equilibrium or saturation/clamping mechanism is observationally equivalent here to a true loading-dependent law whose change is smaller than assay resolution.

## H3 [repeatability and dilution unresolved beyond precipitation]
Batches 11 and 12 ended near the same component concentration (~0.8 mol/L) by staged dilution versus direct preparation. Their final precipitation signals agree closely (0.15148 versus 0.15125; events runner-operation-0056/-0061), while acid fractions differ by 0.0148 and pH_normalized by 0.00247. With only two preparations and instrument noise, this is not evidence for a path effect. The batch-11 pre-dilution pH-meter reading at ~1.6 mol/L versus its post-dilution final assay is also instrument-confounded; it does not establish a dilution response.

## Scope and alternatives
Claims apply only to water, ambient conditions, the tested loading ranges, and these anonymous inputs. Absolute loading versus volume is not separately identifiable because equal-concentration comparisons are sparse and nearly flat overall. Intermediate pH-meter readings showed larger same-state scatter than final assays, so they are qualitative corroboration. The precipitation channel may represent a fixed background, a broad plateau, or a normalized proxy with an onset outside the sampled range. Environment equilibrium confidence/residual were diagnostics, not scientific targets.

## Testable consequence
Within this scope, a new 0.4–0.8 mol/L aqueous preparation should return approximately pH_normalized 0.253, dissociation 0.07, and precipitation 0.153, with deviations assessed against the declared assay noise and preparation-to-preparation scatter. A reproducible shift under much lower loading, a broader dilution range, or orthogonal solubility measurement would overturn the near-constant approximation.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
At equal loading and reaction history, solvent S2 should favor recovery and larger/cleaner crystals because its dossier gives low solubility, high growth, low nucleation, and low occlusion; S1 is the main alternative. A slow seeded cool with a cold hold should reduce fines relative to an unseeded or rapid cool. This is a prior, not experimental evidence.

## H2 [tentative]
Catalyst C1 is the conservative first reaction choice (high nominal activity with modest variability); C3 may outperform it. Initial test: 0.04 mol reagent, 0.08 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, hot reaction, quench/cool, seed, hold, filter. I will change material choice if HPLC/final assays contradict these expectations.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [partly supported]
S2 processes can give very pure crystals, but fines depend strongly on thermal/seeding history. Batch 1 (events 0006–0016) gave purity 0.986 but fines 0.531; batch 2 (0021–0027), using much less seed and a single slower 14,400 s cool, met the fines constraint at 0.480 with purity 0.982. The designs also differed in reaction temperature/time and an intervening warm hold, so the causal contribution of seed dose versus cooling history remains unresolved. I will retain the batch-2 crystallization protocol while screening catalysts.

## H2 [unresolved]
C1/S2 reaction selectivity remained only about 0.47–0.48 in both tested reaction schedules, while conversion was near complete. The numerical differences do not establish a temperature effect. Catalyst identity is now the main test factor; prediction before batches 3–5: C3 or C2 may improve target formation relative to C1, while C0 likely underperforms nominally. A final assay yield increase under otherwise matched conditions will change the preferred catalyst.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [narrowed]
The batch-2 fines success did not generalize across catalysts under the nominally same S2/0.01 g seed/direct slow-cool protocol: batches 3–5 gave fines about 0.590, 0.504, and 0.681. Thus catalyst-dependent composition or uncontrolled process variability materially affects particle outcomes; S2 alone is insufficient to ensure the fines limit. Batch 6 reduced seed to 0.001 g and staged the cool, but fines worsened to 0.612 while size fell, opposing the low-seed hypothesis in the C3/S2 scope. Next tests will change solvent while keeping C3 and the simpler 0.01 g seed slow cool.

## H2 [supported in tested S2 schedule]
C3 produced the highest recovery in the matched catalyst screen: batch 3 crystal yield 0.436 versus C1 0.368, C2 0.303, and C0 0.406; batch 6 repeated C3 at 0.461 despite altered crystallization. C3 therefore remains the reaction lead, although neither C3 batch met the fines constraint. C1 batch 2 is the current feasible fallback.

## H3 [tentative]
S1's lower nominal nucleation and occlusion tendencies may reduce C3 fines, at some recovery cost from higher solubility than S2. S3 is a higher-activity alternative but may worsen purity/occlusion. A feasible C3 solvent result would supersede batch 2 if its recovery exceeds 0.368.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only as solvent ranking for fines]
Changing C3 from S2 to S1 or S3 increased rather than decreased fines (batches 7 and 8: 0.987 and 0.648). C1/S1 also failed at 0.659 (batch 9). Despite S1 giving the highest observed recovery (0.532 with C3), its particle distribution makes it infeasible. The dossier nucleation prior is therefore contradicted for these realized processes; S2 remains preferred for constraint control.

## H2 [supported in tested schedules]
C3 improves reaction/product recovery but creates a recovery–fines tradeoff: C3/S2 yielded 0.436–0.461 with fines 0.590–0.612, whereas feasible C1/S2 batch 2 yielded 0.368 with fines 0.480. Solvent changes raised C3 recovery but did not solve fines.

## H4 [tentative, pre-batch 10]
A high seed dose plus a cooling–reheat–recooling cycle may dissolve fines and regrow remaining crystals, lowering C3/S2 fines below 0.50 while retaining recovery above batch 2. Failure would favor using C1/S2 or testing upstream dilution/loading rather than further solvent changes.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only as solvent ranking for fines]
S2 is the best tested solvent for fines control; S1 and S3 failed clearly under matched C3 schedules.

## H2 [supported with tradeoff]
C3 improves recovery, but standard full loading gave excessive fines. Batch 10's high-seed thermal cycle worsened fines to 0.819, rejecting that remedy in the tested scope.

## H5 [tentative, pre-batch 12]
Reducing C3/S2 reagent loading from 0.04 to 0.03 mol improved selectivity and recovery fraction (batch 11 yield 0.488) and lowered fines to 0.529, though it remained outside specification. A further reduction to 0.02 mol at unchanged solvent, catalyst, seed, and slow cool is predicted to cross the fines limit while retaining recovery above the feasible batch-2 value of 0.368. If it fails, batch 2 remains the only clear feasible recommendation.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested campaign scope]
S2 was the best tested solvent for satisfying particle constraints. S1 increased recovery but produced excessive fines, and S3 also failed the fines limit (batches 7–9).

## H2 [supported with resolved operating condition]
C3 was the strongest recovery catalyst but required reduced upstream reagent loading to control fines. Full-load C3/S2 batches 3 and 6 achieved recovery 0.436–0.461 but fines 0.590–0.612; a high-seed thermal cycle in batch 10 worsened fines to 0.819. Reducing reagent charge to 0.03 mol in batch 11 raised recovery fraction to 0.488 and lowered fines to 0.529, suggesting a loading trend but still failing specification.

## H5 [supported by final test]
At 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L S2, 0.005 mol C3, 330 K/1800 s reaction, 0.01 g seed, and a 270 K/14,400 s cool, batch 12 achieved crystal yield 0.520, purity 0.994, and fines 0.387 (event 0138). This is the highest observed recovery among batches meeting purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. Batch 2 is an independent feasible fallback (yield 0.368, fines 0.480), but it is materially lower recovery.

## Decision
Recommend completed batch 12. Scope caveat: the apparent loading trend has only one batch at each loading, so repeatability and separate catalyst/loading effects remain unresolved; nonetheless the observed final assay satisfies both constraints with appreciable margin.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Catalysts and solvents will materially affect reaction conversion/selectivity; the nominal dossier suggests C1 or C3 and S2/S3 as productive starting points, but fixed residuals could reverse this. A high-temperature reaction followed by quench will test feasibility. If HPLC shows poor conversion or selectivity, vary catalyst before crystallization refinements.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
For crystallization, S2 should favor growth, low impurity occlusion, and low nucleation, so modest seeding plus slow cooling and a cold hold should produce purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. Faster cooling or excess seed is expected to increase fines; insufficient supersaturation may lower recovery. Testable consequence: among otherwise similar runs, slow seeded cooling should improve size/fines, while deeper cold holds should increase recovery.

## Decision scope
First establish a productive upstream recipe and feasible crystallization. Thereafter use batches to separate catalyst, solvent, seed dose, cooling rate, cold endpoint/hold, and (if useful) reheat/recool effects. Final selection will prioritize measured crystal_yield only among batches satisfying both quality constraints.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
At 390 K/3600 s in S2, C0 is the best tested catalyst for usable target formation. Final assays gave crystal_yield 0.452 for C0 (event runner-operation-0057), versus 0.409 C1 (0015), 0.419 C2 (0071), and 0.373 C3 (0043), with all comparable 270 K seeded crystallizations meeting purity/fines constraints except a separate colder run. HPLC directionally agreed that C0 had the highest yield/selectivity among the catalyst screen (0050 versus 0007, 0036, 0064). These are numerical differences under one run each, so catalyst-by-condition interaction and run variability remain unresolved.

## H2 [narrowed]
Seeded slow cooling to 270 K with S2 is repeatedly compatible with high purity and fines below 0.50 (0015, 0043, 0057, 0071). Cooling instead to 265 K produced fines_fraction 1.0 despite similar purity (0029), so deeper cooling can trigger excessive secondary nucleation; this is a large single-run contrast, not yet a repeatability estimate. Test 275 K and thermal-history/seed variants around C0/S2.

## H3 [tentative]
Solvent S2 nominally supports clean growth, but other solvents may improve reaction yield enough to offset crystallization disadvantages. Screen solvents with C0, holding reaction and 270 K crystallization broadly fixed.

## Decision
Use C0 at 390 K/3600 s as current upstream baseline. Prioritize solvent effects, then optimize endpoint/hold and seed strategy. Final selection remains highest measured crystal_yield among purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
At 390 K/3600 s, C0 is the best tested catalyst with S2. The catalyst comparison and HPLC evidence are recorded in events 0015, 0043, 0050/0057, 0064/0071. Interaction outside this condition remains unresolved.

## H2 [supported for solvent quality tradeoff]
Solvent changes create a strong recovery–fines tradeoff. S0 and S1 increased crystal_yield to about 0.54 and 0.53 but failed fines (0.81 and 0.62; events 0113 and 0085). S3 also failed fines and had lower recovery (0099). Slow cooling, warmer endpoints, long holds, and 0.20 g seed did not rescue S0/S1 below the 0.50 fines limit (0130, 0147), suggesting a solvent-specific nucleation tendency rather than only cooling-rate control. S2 remains the reliable quality solvent.

## H3 [supported directionally; final test precommitted]
Within C0/S2, reducing solvent from 0.08 to 0.06 L raised measured crystal_yield from 0.452 (0057) to 0.467 (0161), but fines moved from 0.413 to 0.512, narrowly outside specification. Because these are single runs with assay noise, exact monotonicity is unresolved. Prediction before batch 12: an intermediate 0.065 L loading with the established 270 K slow cooling should preserve most recovery gain while bringing fines below 0.50. A failed fines result will leave batch 4 (event 0057) as the leading confirmed feasible process.

## Final decision rule
Select the completed batch with highest measured crystal_yield among those with crystal_purity >=0.80 and crystal_fines_fraction <=0.50; do not substitute native score for this rule.

# Campaign hypotheses — final source-stage record

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
C0 at 390 K/3600 s was the best tested catalyst with S2 under the common seeded 270 K crystallization. Batch 4 (final assay event runner-operation-0057) gave crystal_yield 0.4525, purity 1.000, and fines 0.4130. Comparable C1, C2, and C3 batches had lower recovery (events 0015, 0071, 0043). Single-run comparisons leave repeatability and interactions unresolved.

## H2 [supported for solvent quality tradeoff]
S0 and S1 improved reaction/overall recovery but strongly worsened number-fines: final crystal_yield/fines were about 0.540/0.811 for S0 (0113) and 0.534/0.622 for S1 (0085). S3 also failed fines (0099). Warmer endpoints, slower cooling, longer holds, and 0.20 g seed did not rescue S0/S1 (0130, 0147). Thus S2 is the best-supported solvent for meeting the quality constraint, despite lower recovery.

## H3 [disconfirmed as a simple interpolation]
The precommitted expectation that intermediate 0.065 L S2 would retain recovery while restoring fines below 0.50 was not supported: batch 12 gave yield 0.4668 but fines 0.6013 (0174). The 0.06 L batch was only narrowly over the limit at 0.5123 (0161), but it is still infeasible by the stated point-estimate rule. These single results and instrument noise mean the loading response is not demonstrably monotone; repeatability would be needed before choosing a boundary recipe.

## Final selection
Recommend lifecycle batch 4. It has the highest measured crystal_yield among completed batches whose final assay satisfies purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. # Working hypotheses

**H1 [supported in tested reaction scope]** C1 with S2, S1, or S0 at ~373 K gives near-complete conversion; S0 produced the highest observed reaction yield (~0.619) and crystal recovery (~0.494), whereas C3/S2 at 363 K was poorer, with catalyst and temperature confounded (runner-operation-0015, -0059, -0118, -0144). # Final source-stage hypotheses

**H1 [supported in tested scope]** Reaction and crystallization are strongly coupled to material identity. S0/C1 gave the largest unconstrained recovery observed (~0.494) but extreme fines (~0.987; runner-operation-0144). S3/C1 sacrifices some recovery but enables a qualitatively different particle regime.

**H2 [rejected as general control strategy]** For S2, larger seed charge, long holding, reheat/recool, and very slow staged cooling did not reduce fines below ~0.98 (runner-operation-0051, -0059, -0079, -0082, -0092 through -0105). These variables cannot be assumed transferable across solvents.

**H3 [supported, narrow process window]** With S3/C1, cooling only to 300 K gave fines ~0.756 (runner-operation-0225), whereas continued cooling to 250 K followed by twelve 4 h low-temperature holds produced purity ~0.976, fines ~0.388, and seed-excluded recovery ~0.427 (runner-operation-0241). The effect is associated with the combined deeper cooling plus long hold; those factors were not separated.

**H4 [supported catalyst specificity]** Repeating the deep-cool/long-hold S3 workup with C0, C2, or C3 did not reproduce compliant fines (all ~0.675–0.693; runner-operation-0265, -0289, -0313). Thus C1 is required within the tested catalyst set, despite C0 giving a numerically higher recovery than C1 under that workup.

**Decision.** Recommend batch 9: it is the only observed batch satisfying both purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50, and its recovery (~0.427) substantially exceeds the initial feasibility target. Key unresolved question is whether the 250 K endpoint or the 48 h hold is the dominant cause; either change could invalidate compliance.
